Randomized Projection Methods in Linear Algebra and Data Analysis  SIAMRandomized Projection Methods in Linear Algebra and Data Analysis | SIAM SIAM｡Randomized Projection Methods in Linear Algebra and Data Analysis Per-Gunnar Martinsson The management and analysis of large complex datasets give rise to mathematical and algorithmic challenges that have intrigued applied mathematicians in recent years. A common situation is a dataset that apparently lives in high-dimensional space, even though evidence suggests that it is interpretable as having a lower “intrinsic” dimension. Finding a way to represent such a dataset using fewer parameters enables its efficient storage, transmission, and analysis to uncover additional structures. Informally, one might say that the difficulty that arises as a problem’s dimensionality grows is that there are just too many places to look. The unit cube in Rn has 2n corners, which is a lot even for, say, n=100. Curiously, one’s best bet when facing a vast search space such as this is often to conduct the search completely randomly. I will illustrate how this works in practice by reviewing two recently developed algorithms — one for factorizing matrices and the other for finding approximate nearest neighbors. Linear Approximation (Principal Component Analysis) A classical and well-understood dimension reduction problem—given a set of points {aj}j=1n in Rm—is to find a linear subspace L that to some degree of approximation contains all points. A common technique for finding L is to form the m×n matrix A=[a1,a2,…,an] and compute its singular value decomposition (SVD) A=∑j=1pσjujvj∗, where p=min(m,n), {σj}j=1p are the singular values of A (ordered so σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σp≥0), and {uj}j=1p and {vj}j=1p are the left and right singular vectors of A. For any k∈{1,2,…,p}, the subspace L spanned by the first k left singular vectors {uj}j=1k is in certain regards “optimal.” The aforementioned problem arises in many applications. An example occurs in statistics, when one attempts to fit observed high-dimensional data to an assumption that such data represent samples drawn from a multivariate normal distribution driven by a small number of significant components. Randomized SVD The problem of finding an optimal linear subspace has a clean and simple mathematical solution, but a user must determine how to compute the dominant k singular values and singular vectors of the given data matrix A. Standard linear algebra routines, such as those in LAPACK, often return the full decomposition. This computation’s flop count, O(mnmin(m,n)), is typically unaffordable for large matrices. Alternatively, one could compute a partial factorization using an algorithm like column pivoted QR or Arnoldi. While this would reduce the asymptotic flop count to O(mnk), these algorithms can be difficult to efficiently implement on modern communication-constrained hardware. Another option, which is often highly competitive, is the recently-developed randomized SVD (RSVD) [1], which draws a Gaussian random matrix G of size n×k to create a sampling matrix Y=AG. In many situations, the columns of matrix Y form a good approximate basis for the column space of A. To identify approximations to the dominant modes of an SVD of A, one must orthonormalize Y's columns to find a basis for its column space before projecting the matrix A down to this subspace and using deterministic methods to compute a full SVD of the resulting small matrix. To attain accuracy comparable to the best possible approximation of rank k, the RSVD must draw a few extra samples. To this end, let us select an oversampling parameter p (p=5 or p=10 are generally good) and proceed as follows: Draw an n×(k+p) Gaussian random matrix G Form the m×(k+p) sampling matrix Y=AG Form an m×(k+p) orthonormal matrix Q, such that Y=QR Form the (k+p)×n matrix B=Q∗A Compute a (small) SVD B=U^DV∗ Form the matrix U=QU^. The result is an approximate factorization A≈UDV∗, where the diagonal matrix D holds approximations to the singular vectors of A and the tall, thin matrices U and V have orthonormal columns. The RSVD has the same O(mnk) complexity as existing techniques for partial SVD computation. However, its interaction with the matrix A via two matrix-matrix multiplications offers compelling advantages, as it often leads to high practical execution speed. Furthermore, it eases the method’s use in situations where A may be stored on slow memory, such as a hard drive, or across a distributed computing system. The RSVD produces a factorization with near-optimal accuracy in scenarios where A's singular values decay reasonably rapidly.siam.org4. Randomized Algorithms for Low-rankRandomized Algorithms for Low-rank arXiv｡ 2.4. Randomized SVD. It is well-known that computing the full SVD of a matrix costs O(mn2), assuming m ≥ n. When the dimensions of a matrix X ∈ Rm×n are very large, the computational cost of a full SVD may be prohibitively expensive. Randomized SVD, popularized by [24], is a computationally eﬃcient way to compute a rank-r approximation of a matrix X. Assuming that X is approximately low-rank or has singular values that decay rapidly, the randomized SVD delivers a good low-rank representation of the matrix. Compared to the full SVD, the randomized SVD is much more computationally eﬃcient across a wide- range of matrices. We now describe the randomized SVD algorithm for computing a rank-r approximation to X, where the target rank 1 ≤ r ≤ rank(X). The randomized algorithm has two distinct stages—the range ﬁnding stage, and the postprocessing stage to compute the low-rank ap- proximation. In the range ﬁnding stage, we ﬁrst draw a random matrix Ω ∈ Rn×(r+p), where r is the desired target rank, and p is a small nonnegative integer used as an oversampling pa- rameter. While many choices for the distribution of Ω are possible, in this paper, we use the Gaussian distribution, i.e., the entries Ωij are independent and identically distributed N(0, 1) random variables. Then, we compute the matrix Y = XΩ whose columns consist of random linear combinations of the columns of X. By taking a thin QR factorization Y = QR, we get a matrix Q with orthonormal columns whose span approximates the range of X. If the matrix X is approximately rank r, R(Q) is a good approximation for R(X) as the range of X is characterized by just the ﬁrst r left singular vectors. We can then express X ≈ QQ X. In the second stage, we convert the low rank representation into the SVD format. To this end, we compute the thin SVD of B = Q X, giving B = UBΣV . We truncate this representation to rank r by only retaining the ﬁrst r diagonal elements of Σ and drop the corresponding columns from UB and V. Finally, we compute U = QUB, and obtain the low-rank approximation X = UΣV . Algorithm 2.1 summarizes the process. 6 Algorithm 2.1 [U, Σ, V] = RandSVD(X, r, p, Ω) Input: matrix X ∈ Rm×n, target rank r, oversampling parameter p ≥ 0 such that r + p ≤ min{m, n}, Gaussian random matrix Ω ∈ Rn×(r+p) Output: U ∈ Rm×r, Σ ∈ Rr×r, and V ∈ Rn×r such that X ≈ UΣV 1: Multiply Y ← XΩ 2: Thin QR factorization Y = QR 3: Form B ← Q X 4: Calculate thin SVD B = UBΣV 5: Form U ← QUB(: , 1 : r) 6: Compress Σ ← Σ(1 : r, 1 : r), and V ← V(: , 1 : r) We brieﬂy review the computational cost of the RandSVD algorithm. Let T denote the computational cost of a matrix-vector product (denoted matvec) involving the matrix X. Then, the cost of the algorithm is Cost = 2(r + p)O(nnz(X)) + O(r2 (m + n)), where nnz denotes the number of nonzeros of X. An error bound for Algorithm 2.1 in the Frobenius norm is presented below, and we will use this result frequently in our analysis. This theorem and its proof can be found in [46, Theorem 3]. Theorem 2.4. Let X ∈ Rm×n, and Ω ∈ Rn×(r+p) be a Gaussian random matrix. Suppose Q is obtained from Algorithm 2.1 with inputs target rank r and oversampling parameter p ≥ 2 such that r + p ≤ min{m, n}, and let Br be the rank-r truncated SVD of Q X. Then, the error in expectation satisﬁes EΩ X − QQ X 2 F ≤ EΩ X − QBr 2 F ≤ 1 + r p − 1 min{m,n} j=r+1 σ2 j (X). Remark 1. We will use two slightly diﬀerent formulations of this theorem in our later results. Instead of X − QBr 2 F , we will use X − UU X 2 F .arxiv.org5. The computational time can be further reduced by ﬁrst computing the QR decomposition of B and then computing the SVD of the even smaller matrix R ∈ Rl×l or via the eigendecomposition of the l × l matrix BB (see Voronin and Martinsson (2015) and Section 3.4 for further details). Error bounds. The randomized algorithm for the low-rank SVD only approximates Ak, the actual rank-k truncated SVD, obtained from the full SVD of A. The error bounds are worse than the optimal ones given in (4), but the practical results tend to be very close to optimal. In the algorithm in Figure 8, we compute the full SVD of B, so it follows that A−UkSkVk = A−QQ A . In Halko et al. (2011b), the following error bound is derived: E A − UkSkVk ≤ 1 + k p − 1 σ2q+1 k+1 + e √ k + p p j>k σ 2(2q+1) j 1 2 1 2q+1 When the singular values σj for j > k are small in magnitude, the sum in the above formula is small and the bound approaches the theoretically optimal value of σk+1 with increasing q. Note again that the error in the appoximate low rank SVD factorization obtained with the randomized algorithm coincides with the bound A − QQ A . To control the error, one may proceed to buildup Q by adding samples to expand Y a step at a time, until the bound becomes small. A more intricate iterative procedure for building up Q such that the bound holds to a speciﬁed tolerance is presented in Martinsson and Voronin (2015). 3.3. Measurement matrices. An essential computational step of the randomized algorithm is to construct a measurement matrix Ω that is used to sample the range of the input matrix. Therefore we rely on the properties of random vectors, which imply that the randomly generated columns of the measurement matrix are linearly independent with high probability. Indeed, this includes the whole class of sub-Gaussian random variables (Rivasplata 2012), including matrices with Bernoulli or uniform random entries. Due to its attractive theoretical properties, the random Gaussian measurement matrix is the most prominent choice, consisting of independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) N(0, 1) standard normal entries. In practice, however, uniform random measurements are suﬃcient and are less expensive to generate. The drawback is that dense vector and matrix operations are expensive for large matrices. However, BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) operations tend to be highly scalable and computations could be substantially accelerated with parallel or distributed processing, e.g., a graphics processing unit (GPU) implementation (Erichson and Donovan 2016; Voronin and Martinsson 2015). Woolfe et al. (2008) proposed another computationally eﬃcient approach, exploiting the properties of a structured random measurement matrix.arxiv.org6. Lecture 16: Matrix functions. Randomized SVD: A Deep DiveRandomized SVD: A Deep Dive Number Analytics｡Randomized SVD: A Deep Dive Exploring the Theoretical and Practical Aspects of Randomized Singular Value Decomposition Introduction Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) is a fundamental technique in numerical linear algebra, widely used in various fields such as data compression, image processing, and machine learning. However, traditional SVD methods can be computationally expensive for large-scale matrices. Randomized SVD has emerged as a powerful alternative, offering significant improvements in efficiency and scalability. In this article, we will delve into the world of Randomized SVD, exploring its theoretical foundations, practical implementations, and real-world applications. Advanced Theoretical Topics Detailed Analysis of Randomized Algorithms for SVD Randomized SVD algorithms are based on the idea of approximating the SVD of a matrix by applying random projections to the matrix. The resulting low-rank approximation can be computed efficiently using traditional SVD methods. One of the most popular randomized SVD algorithms is the Randomized Singular Value Decomposition (RSVD) algorithm, which is based on the following steps: Generate a random matrix Ω \mathbf{\Omega} Ω of size n×k n \times k n×k, where k k k is the desired rank. Compute the matrix product Y=AΩ \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{\Omega} Y=AΩ, where A \mathbf{A} A is the input matrix. Compute the QR decomposition of Y \mathbf{Y} Y to obtain Q \mathbf{Q} Q and R \mathbf{R} R. Compute the SVD of QTA \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A} QTA to obtain U \mathbf{U} U, Σ \mathbf{\Sigma} Σ, and V \mathbf{V} V. The RSVD algorithm can be summarized in the following flowchart: Generate random matrix Ω Compute Y = AΩ Compute QR decomposition of Y Compute SVD of Q^T A Output U, Σ, V Discussion of Error Bounds and Convergence Rates The accuracy of Randomized SVD algorithms depends on the quality of the random projections. The error bounds for Randomized SVD can be analyzed using the following theorem: Theorem 1 1: Let A \mathbf{A} A be a matrix of size m×n m \times n m×n and Ω \mathbf{\Omega} Ω be a random matrix of size n×k n \times k n×k. Then, with high probability, the error bound for the RSVD algorithm is given by: \[|\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^T|F \leq \sqrt{1 + \frac{k}{p-k-1}}\sigma{k+1}(\mathbf{A})\] where σk+1(A) \sigma_{k+1}(\mathbf{A}) σk+1(A) is the (k+1) (k+1) (k+1)-th singular value of A \mathbf{A} A and p p p is the number of power iterations. Comparison with Traditional SVD Methods Traditional SVD methods, such as the Jacobi SVD algorithm, can be computationally expensive for large-scale matrices. Randomized SVD algorithms, on the other hand, offer significant improvements in efficiency and scalability. A comparison of the computational complexity of different SVD algorithms is given in the following table: Algorithm Computational Complexity Jacobi SVD O(mn2) O(mn^2) O(mn2) RSVD O(mnk) O(mnk) O(mnk) Randomized Power Iteration SVD O(mnk+nk2) O(mnk + nk^2) O(mnk+nk2) Real-World Applications Case Studies of Randomized SVD in Data Compression and Image Processing Randomized SVD has been widely used in data compression and image processing applications. For example, in image compression, Randomized SVD can be used to reduce the dimensionality of the image data, resulting in significant compression ratios. A case study of Randomized SVD in image compression is given in 2. Applications in Latent Semantic Analysis and Topic Modeling Randomized SVD has also been used in latent semantic analysis and topic modeling applications. For example, in latent semantic analysis, Randomized SVD can be used to reduce the dimensionality of the term-document matrix, resulting in improved document clustering and retrieval performance. A case study of Randomized SVD in latent semantic analysis is given in 3. Use Cases in Scientific Computing and Machine Learning Randomized SVD has been widely used in scientific computing and machine learning applications. For example, in machine learning, Randomized SVD can be used to reduce the dimensionality of the feature space, resulting in improved model performance and reduced training times.numberanalytics.com8. Outline of the tutorial: 1. Techniques for computing the SVD of a matrix of exact rank k. 2. Variations of techniques for matrices of exact rank. • Single pass algorithms. • How to compute spanning rows and spanning columns (CUR, etc). 3. Techniques for matrices of the form A = EF + N with N small. • Error estimation. 4. Techniques for matrices of the form A = EF + N with N large. • The “power method.” 5. Random transforms that can be applied rapidly. • The “Subsampled Random Fourier Transform” (SRFT) and its cousins. 6. Review / Putting things together / Model problems. We are faced with a problem: • The randomized algorithm performs poorly for large matrices whose singular values decay slowly. • The matrices of interest to us are large and have slowly decaying singular values. What to do? Idea [Rokhlin, Szlam, Tygert 2008]: Apply the algorithm to the auxiliary matrix B = (A A∗ )q A. The matrices A and B have the same left singular vectors, and the singular values of B decay much faster. In fact: σj(B) = (σj(A))2 q+1 . So use the sample matrix Z = B Ω = (A A∗ )q A Ω instead of Y = A Ω. Algorithm for computing a rank-k SVD of a given matrix A: (1) Pick a parameter p and set = k + p. Draw an n × random matrix Ω. (2) Compute a sample matrix Y = AA∗ q AΩ. Note: The product is typically evaluated via alternating applications of A and A∗. (3) Compute an orthonormal matrix Q such that Y = QQ∗Y. Then with high probability, A ≈ QQ∗A. (4) Form B = Q∗ A. (5) Factorize B = ˆ UΣV∗. (6) Form U = Qˆ U. (7) If desired, truncate the -term SVD A = UΣV∗ to its leading k terms. Output: A factorization A ≈ UΣV∗. Power method for improving accuracy: Theorem: [Halko, Martinsson, Tropp 2009] Let m, n, and be positive integers such that < n ≤ m. Let A be an m × n matrix and let Ω be an n × matrix. Let q be a non-negative integer, set B = (AA∗)q A, and construct the sample matrix Z = B Ω. Let PZ denote the orthogonal projector onto the range of Z. Then ||(I − PZ) A|| ≤ ||(I − PZ) B||1/(2q+1) . Since the ’th singular value of B = (AA∗)q A is σ2 q+1 , any result of the type ||(I − PY) A|| ≤ C σk+1, where Y = A Ω and C = C(m, n, k), gets improved to a result ||(I − PZ) A|| ≤ C1/(2 q+1) σk+1 when Z = (AA∗)q A Ω. We note that the new power method can be viewed as a hybrid between the “basic” randomized method, and a Krylov subspace method: Krylov method: Restrict A to the linear space Vq(ω) = Span(Aω, A2 ω,Aq ω). “Basic” randomized method: Restrict A to the linear space Span(Aω1, Aω2,Aω ) = V1(ω1) × V1(ω2)V1(ω ). “Power” method: Restrict A to the linear space Span(Aq ω1, Aq ω2,Aq ω ). Modiﬁed “power” method: Restrict A to the linear space Vq(ω1) × Vq(ω2)Vq(ω ). This could be a promising area for further work. Example 1: The matrix A being analyzed is a 9025 × 9025 matrix arising in a diﬀusion geometry approach to image processing. To be precise, A is a graph Laplacian on the manifold of 9 × 9 patches. j Approximation error e Estimated Eigenvalues λj Magnitude “Exact” eigenvalues λj for q = 3 λj for q = 2 λj for q = 1 λj for q = 0 The parameter q is the “power” in the “power method”. Note the speed with which accuracy improves!amath.colorado.edu1. On Transferring Transferability: Towards a Theory for Size GeneralizationOn Transferring Transferability: Towards a Theory for Size Generalization｡On Transferring Transferability: Towards a Theory for Size Generalization Eitan Levin⋄,,,\diamond Department of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, Caltech, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA. Yuxin Ma22footnotemark: 2⋄,,,\diamond Mateo Díaz Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics and the Mathematical Institute for Data Science, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD 21218, USA. Soledad Villar22footnotemark: 2 Abstract Many modern learning tasks require models that can take inputs of varying sizes. Consequently, dimension-independent architectures have been proposed for domains where the inputs are graphs, sets, and point clouds. Recent work on graph neural networks has explored whether a model trained on low-dimensional data can transfer its performance to higher-dimensional inputs. We extend this body of work by introducing a general framework for transferability across dimensions. We show that transferability corresponds precisely to continuity in a limit space formed by identifying small problem instances with equivalent large ones. This identification is driven by the data and the learning task. We instantiate our framework on existing architectures, and implement the necessary changes to ensure their transferability. Finally, we provide design principles for designing new transferable models. Numerical experiments support our findings. $\diamond$$\diamond$footnotetext: These authors contributed equally to this work Contents 1 Introduction 2 How to consistently grow: equivalence of differently sized objects 1. 2.1 How to define distances across dimensions 3 Transferability is just continuity 1. 4 Transferability implies size generalization 5 Transferable neural networks 5.1 Sets 5.2 Graphs 1. 5.3 Point clouds 6 Size generalization experiments Acknowledgments 1. For instance, graph neural networks (GNN) for graphs [61], DeepSet for sets [82], and PointNet for point clouds [56]. These models have a desirable feature: they can be trained with low-dimensional samples and, then, deployed on higher-dimensional data. Numerical experiments support our findings. ∗ Department of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, Caltech, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA. † Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics and the Mathematical Institute for Data Science, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD 21218, USA. ⋄ These authors contributed equally to this work 1 Contents 1 Introduction 3 2 How to consistently grow: equivalence of differently sized objects 5 2.1 How to define distances across dimensions 7 3 Transferability is just continuity 7 4 Transferability implies size generalization 8 5 Transferable neural networks 9 5.1 Sets 9 5.2 Graphs 10 5.3 Point clouds 11 6 Size generalization experiments 12 Acknowledgments 14 References 14 A Notation 19 B Consistent sequences and compatible, transferable maps: details and missing proofs from Section 2 20 C Transferability: details and missing proofs from Section 3 26 D Generalization bounds: details and missing proofs from Section 4 31 E Example 1 (sets): details and missing proofs from Section 5.1 35 F Example 2 (graphs): details and missing proofs from Section 5.2 44 G Example 3 (point clouds): details and missing proofs from Section 5.3 55 H Size generalization experiments: details from Section 6 62 I Limitations of this work 69 2 1 Introduction Modern learning problems often involve inputs of arbitrary size: language has text sequences of arbitrary length, graphs encode networks with an arbitrary number of nodes, and particle systems might have an arbitrary number of points. Although traditional models are typically limited to the specific input dimensions they were trained on, dimension-independent architectures have been proposed for several domains. For instance, graph neural networks (GNN) for graphs [61], DeepSet for sets [82], and PointNet for point clouds [56]. These models have a desirable feature: they can be trained with low-dimensional samples and, then, deployed on higher-dimensional data. A key question in this context is whether the performance of a model trained with low-dimensional samples transfers across dimensions. This has been thoroughly studied in the context of GNNs [61, 50, 51], where the term transferability was first coined. In turn, the tools used to establish transferability of GNNs are, at first sight, problem-specific, including the concept of a graphon, and certain convergence of homomorphism densities. Thus, the analysis does not readily extend beyond GNNs, and so we ask What properties of the model, data, and learning task ensure that learning performance transfers well across dimensions? This question is relevant for the current pursuit of graph foundation models [46], GNN for combinatorial optimization [9], neural PDE solvers [57, 44], and so on, where pre-trained models aim to be adapted to a wide range of tasks involving different-sized objects. In this paper, we answer this question by identifying assumptions on the learning problem that make a model generalize across dimensions, and give a theoretical framework to understand models with such properties. Our framework requires technical notions that we develop throughout the paper, so before diving into the details, we proceed to give the high-level intuition. Our framework considers a machine learning model parametrized by θ ∈ Rk, where the number of parameters k is fixed. For any fixed θ, the model can be evaluated on inputs of any size n. That is, the learned θ defines a sequence of functions, for example, (fn : Vn → R)n with increasingly larger input sizes.1 We think of Vn ⊆ V∞ as a subspace of an infinite-dimensional limit space.arxiv.org1. Multilevel Diffusion: Infinite Dimensional Score-Based Diffusion Models for Image Generation — LacunaMultilevel Diffusion: Infinite Dimensional Score-Based Diffusion Models for Image Generation — Lacuna｡Multilevel Diffusion: Infinite Dimensional Score-Based Diffusion Models for Image Generation Paul Hagemann, Lars Ruthotto, Gabriele Steidl, Nicole Tianjiao Yang, Yang, Nicole Tianjiao arXiv 2023 · DOI · DBLP Abstract Traditional Score-Based Diffusion Models (SBDMs) are typically constrained to fixed-resolution image tensors, leading to theoretical inconsistencies and practical limitations when scaling to higher resolutions. This paper introduces a novel framework that formulates SBDMs in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. By utilizing trace-class covariance operators and resolution-independent Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs), the authors enable "multilevel training." This approach allows models to generalize across resolutions and provides a mathematically grounded method for warm-starting high-resolution training from low-resolution precursors. Introduction Most state-of-the-art generative models treat images as discrete, fixed-size grids (e.g., 32×3232 \times 3232×32 or 256×256256 \times 256256×256 pixels). While this approach has yielded impressive results, it tethers the model to a specific discretization. From a mathematical perspective, this formulation is ill-posed in the infinite-dimensional limit: as the number of pixels ddd approaches infinity, the energy of standard Gaussian noise (the trace of the identity matrix) also approaches infinity. Consequently, models trained at one resolution often fail to generalize to others without significant retraining or the use of heuristic upsamplers. To address this, the authors propose treating images as continuous functions residing in a separable Hilbert space. This shift from discrete tensors to continuous function spaces allows for a consistent mathematical framework that remains valid across any resolution. Theoretical Framework: Beyond the Identity Crisis The core innovation of this work lies in the definition of forward and reverse diffusion processes using Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) in infinite dimensions. The authors identify a primary culprit in the scaling failure of traditional models: the choice of identity covariance (Q=IdQ=IdQ=Id). In infinite dimensions, identity noise is not well-defined because it lacks a finite trace. To resolve this, the researchers replace the standard identity covariance with trace-class covariance operators. These operators, often based on the Laplacian or Bessel potentials, act as low-pass filters. They ensure that the latent noise distribution remains well-defined even as the resolution increases, effectively "taming" the noise energy in the infinite-dimensional limit. Resolution-Invariant Architectures Standard neural architectures like U-Nets are inherently sensitive to input resolution. To maintain the integrity of the infinite-dimensional formulation, the authors employ Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs). Unlike CNNs, FNOs learn mappings between function spaces by operating in the frequency domain. This allows the model to learn the underlying structure of the data (the "digit function") rather than just the pixel values. This architecture is naturally resolution-invariant, enabling the model to process inputs at any discretization level. Multilevel Training Strategy The authors introduce a multilevel training strategy to improve computational efficiency. The process involves: Training a model on coarse, low-resolution data. Using the weights of the low-resolution model as a "warm start" for training on finer, high-resolution data. This approach is theoretically supported by proofs showing that the discretized models converge to the true infinite-dimensional process. This ensures that the transition between resolutions is mathematically consistent rather than a mere empirical trick. Experimental Results The framework was evaluated across synthetic data, handwritten digits (MNIST), and complex physical simulations (2D Reaction-Diffusion equations). Zero-Shot Super-Resolution A significant finding was the model's capacity for zero-shot super-resolution. An FNO-based model trained exclusively on 32×3232 \times 3232×32 MNIST images successfully generated recognizable digits at 64×6464 \times 6464×64 and 128×128128 \times 128128×128 resolutions without any additional training. In contrast, standard U-Net architectures failed completely, producing only unstructured noise when tested at higher resolutions. Training Efficiency Multilevel training demonstrated clear practical benefits. In MNIST experiments, warm-starting a 64×6464 \times 6464×64 model with weights from a 32×3232 \times 3232×32 model reduced total training time by approximately 9% while maintaining or improving sample quality. This suggests a path toward more sustainable scaling of large generative models.lacuna.tiptreesystems.com3. Any-dimensional equivariant neural networks — LacunaAny-dimensional equivariant neural networks — Lacuna｡Any-dimensional equivariant neural networks Eitan Levin, Mateo Díaz AISTATS 2024 · DBLP Standard neural networks are typically constrained to the input dimensions they were trained on. A model trained on 28×2828\times2828×28 images cannot natively process 50×5050\times5050×50 inputs without resizing or cropping. However, many fundamental problems—from physics to graph theory—are inherently dimension-agnostic. This paper introduces a framework for training "free" equivariant neural networks that generalize across dimensions by leveraging representation stability. The Challenge of Dimension-Agnostic Learning Many real-world mappings are naturally defined for any input size. For instance, the laws of physics apply regardless of the number of particles, and graph properties like "max-cut" are well-defined for any number of nodes. Most current architectures are "locked" into a specific dimension. This research addresses how to learn mappings that accept inputs of any dimension in a mathematically rigorous way, avoiding the "hacks" typically used to handle varying input sizes. Methodology: Equivariance and Stability The proposed framework combines two core concepts: Equivariance: Ensuring the model respects symmetries (e.g., if you permute particles, the output should permute or remain invariant). Representation Stability: A concept from algebraic topology suggesting that for certain group sequences (like permutations SnS_nSn), the structure of equivariant maps stabilizes as nnn grows. The "secret sauce" is a compatibility constraint (CompNNCompNNCompNN). The authors found that simply making a network extendable often leads to poor generalization. The compatibility condition ensures that applying the function in a low dimension is mathematically consistent with extending it to a high dimension and then applying it. The architecture of any-dimensional equivariant networks, showing how layers are lifted across dimensions while maintaining compatibility. Source, p. 3 The training process follows a four-stage "recipe": Identify Symmetry: Determine the relevant symmetry group (e.g., permutations for sets). Find Basis: Establish a basis for equivariant layers at a training dimension n0n_0n0. Train: Optimize the model on data of size n0n_0n0. Lift: To use the model on a new size nnn, solve a sparse linear system to "lift" the learned weights. Experimental Results The authors evaluated the approach on five synthetic tasks: Trace, Diagonal Extraction, Symmetric Projection, Top Singular Vector, and an Orthogonal Invariance task. Training was conducted at a small fixed dimension (e.g., d=4d=4d=4), and testing spanned a range of dimensions. Performance comparison across five tasks. The "Compatible" networks (blue) maintain low error across dimensions, while "Free" networks (orange) without the compatibility constraint fail significantly outside their training dimension (indicated by the vertical dashed line). Source, p. 8 The results demonstrate a stark contrast: Consistent Generalization: Compatible networks maintained low Mean Squared Error (MSE) (e.g., ∼10−8\sim 10^{-8}∼10−8 for Trace) across all tested dimensions. Failure of Naive Extension: Without the compatibility constraint, errors exploded by factors as high as 101010^{10}1010 when moving away from the training dimension. Stability Plateaus: The complexity of the mapping (e.g., the number of parameters) remains constant after a certain point, confirming that the "structure" of these problems stabilizes. Conclusion and Future Directions This framework provides a "black box" approach for any problem with known underlying symmetries. While powerful, it faces challenges in scaling to extremely high dimensions due to the need for solving large sparse linear systems. Future work aims to extend this to non-reductive groups (including translations) and to provide theoretical bounds on generalization error for any-dimensional problems.lacuna.tiptreesystems.com5. [Literature Review] Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization[Literature Review] Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization Moonlight｡[Literature Review] Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization TL;DR Solve length generalization issues with the new LDHD framework, enabling robust scaling from low-dimensional training to high-dimensional data. The paper "Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization and Its Implications for Length Generalization" by Yang Chen, Yitao Liang, and Zhouchen Lin explores a novel theoretical framework termed Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension (LDHD) generalization. This framework is positioned within the broader context of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization, highlighting the scaling challenges that arise when training models on low-dimensional data that must later generalize to high-dimensional spaces. Core Methodology The fundamental assumption guiding the approach is that instances of a problem can be represented as being generated from a latent variable. The dimensionality of this latent variable is suggested to correspond to the complexity or scale of a problem. The authors articulate a specific pathway by which challenges associated with length generalization—the ability to extend understanding from smaller, more manageable instances to larger, more complex ones—can be linked to this low-to-high dimensionality. In essence, the proposed LDHD generalization contextualizes the learning task as follows: Data Generation Process: The data generation for an instance of scale n n n takes place through: Sampling a latent variable h h h from a low-dimensional subspace Σn Σ^n Σn. Determining the output label y y y from this latent variable and an associated concept c c c, where y=c(h) y = c(h) y=c(h). Mapping h h h into a structured input sequence using a data format mapping ϕ ϕ ϕ. Generalizing from Low to High Dimensions: Training occurs with instances sampled from a lower-dimensional subspace, while testing is carried out in a larger, more complex high-dimensional superspace. This setup is characterized by an inherent mismatch, making it difficult for models to leverage learned experiences from training data when applied to testing scenarios. Theoretical Foundations The paper extends traditional definitions relevant to PAC learning theory to include this context of dimensional shifts. It derives a No-Free-Lunch Theorem specific to LDHD generalization, claiming that generalization across these dimensional domains cannot reliably be achieved without prior knowledge about the problem structure, which acts as an inductive bias effectively guiding learning. To substantiate this claim, the authors focus on the implications of different model architectures trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD), investigating their convergence properties and inductive biases. Notably, they explore how some architectures (like random feature models and their projections) capture concepts as min-degree interpolators—meaning they learn to represent functions with minimal polynomial degree necessary for accuracy. Empirical Studies and Model Architecture Central to their investigation is a detailed analysis of specific architectures under SGD such as: Random Feature Models with Projection: These models illustrate how transformations on input data can impact model convergence on certain functions—specifically showing that they converge on min-degree interpolators in relevant function classes. Position-Only Linear Attention with Advice (PLAA): An architecture that minimizes complexity by focusing purely on positional embeddings. The study shows that the reminiscences of understanding long-term dependencies of sequences diminish when using absolute position embeddings; this is remedied by implementing relative position embeddings, which have shown to foster generalization significantly. The outcomes from experiments compare models trained with varying position embedding strategies, notably distinguishing between standard relative position embeddings (RPE) and a novel adaptation termed RPE-Square. The latter is proposed to better handle the nuisances of data formats in the context of achieving length generalization—a key challenge elucidated through the theoretical insights of LDHD generalization. Summary of Contributions The paper presents several key contributions: It formalizes the LDHD generalization framework, tying it closely to length generalization challenges present in various reasoning tasks. Establishes the necessity of utilizing prior structure through appropriate inductive bias to achieve LDHD generalization. Delivers insights into how different model architectures interact with this generalization phenomenon, specifically under SGD optimizations. Proposes the RPE-Square, providing a specific solution targeting the nuances of data formats and general length reasoning. Ultimately, the authors contend that the LDHD framework not only helps clarify the intricacies associated with length generalization but also suggests actionable pathways for future model designs and embedding strategies directed at enhancing generalization capabilities across varied reasoning tasks. They outline implications for further research, particularly in refining inductive biases and developing robust models adaptable to complex generalization challenges.themoonlight.io7. [论文评述] Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization[论文评述] Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization Moonlight｡AI解决低维训练到高维测试的泛化难题,揭示模型设计与长度泛化的核心｡ 该论文提出了一种新的学习方法,称为低维到高维的泛化(Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension, LDHD)泛化｡LDHD泛化是一种特殊的分布外(Out-of-Distribution, OOD)泛化情况,在这种情况下,训练数据被限制在高维测试空间的低维子空间内｡研究者假设每个实例是由潜在变量生成的,并且潜在变量的维度反映了问题的规模｡ 核心方法论详解 理论证明: 论文中证明了LDHD泛化通常无法实现,除非利用先验知识来提供适当的归纳偏见｡具体而言,论文探讨了布尔函数中的LDHD泛化,验证了不同架构在(随机梯度下降)SGD下收敛到不同独立集的最小度插值｡LDHD泛化仅当目标函数与这种归纳偏见一致时才能实现｡ 潜在空间的结构: 研究者指出,许多推理问题中的实例可以看作是从某个潜在空间生成的,其维度反映了问题的规模｡在此背景下,提出了一个数据生成过程的假设: 从维度为n的子空间Σn中采样潜在变量h｡ 标签y由概念c和潜在变量h决定,例如,y = c(h)｡ 隐藏变量h通过数据格式映射ϕ转化为输入序列｡ 纵向与横向的变换: LDHD泛化的主要挑战在于测试空间比训练空间多出维度｡由于测试空间包含与训练空间正交的额外维度,训练样本无法提供有关这些维度如何贡献结果的信息｡因此,研究者引入了LDHD泛化的重要性,使其成为理解长度泛化问题的核心｡ 无免费午餐定理: 论文提出了LDHD泛化的无免费午餐定理,假设不存在普遍的算法能够总是从低维训练数据中学习到目标概念｡为了解决这一问题,研究者探讨了不同模型架构在(S)GD训练下的归纳偏见,试图找出一种结构,使其在低维和高维之间实现有效泛化｡ 模型架构实验: 论文中,研究者分析了随机特征模型(Random Feature Model, RFM)及其变体(随机特征模型和投影,RFMP),证明不同的模型架构能够在不同的独立集上收敛到最小度插值｡此外,研究了仅基于位置的线性注意力(Position-Only Linear Attention with Advice, PLAA)的模型,并通过位置嵌入设计(如RPE和新提出的RPE-Square)展示了如何改进长度泛化｡ 链式思维(CoT)对长度泛化的影响: 论文中还讨论了链式思维如何帮助长度泛化｡themoonlight.io5. To substantiate this claim, the authors focus on the implications of different model architectures trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD), investigating their convergence properties and inductive biases. Notably, they explore how some architectures (like random feature models and their projections) capture concepts as min-degree interpolators—meaning they learn to represent functions with minimal polynomial degree necessary for accuracy. Empirical Studies and Model Architecture Central to their investigation is a detailed analysis of specific architectures under SGD such as: Random Feature Models with Projection: These models illustrate how transformations on input data can impact model convergence on certain functions—specifically showing that they converge on min-degree interpolators in relevant function classes. Position-Only Linear Attention with Advice (PLAA): An architecture that minimizes complexity by focusing purely on positional embeddings. The study shows that the reminiscences of understanding long-term dependencies of sequences diminish when using absolute position embeddings; this is remedied by implementing relative position embeddings, which have shown to foster generalization significantly. The outcomes from experiments compare models trained with varying position embedding strategies, notably distinguishing between standard relative position embeddings (RPE) and a novel adaptation termed RPE-Square. The latter is proposed to better handle the nuisances of data formats in the context of achieving length generalization—a key challenge elucidated through the theoretical insights of LDHD generalization. Summary of Contributions The paper presents several key contributions: It formalizes the LDHD generalization framework, tying it closely to length generalization challenges present in various reasoning tasks. Establishes the necessity of utilizing prior structure through appropriate inductive bias to achieve LDHD generalization. Delivers insights into how different model architectures interact with this generalization phenomenon, specifically under SGD optimizations. Proposes the RPE-Square, providing a specific solution targeting the nuances of data formats and general length reasoning. Ultimately, the authors contend that the LDHD framework not only helps clarify the intricacies associated with length generalization but also suggests actionable pathways for future model designs and embedding strategies directed at enhancing generalization capabilities across varied reasoning tasks. They outline implications for further research, particularly in refining inductive biases and developing robust models adaptable to complex generalization challenges.themoonlight.io7. On Transferring Transferability: Towards a Theory for Size GeneralizationOn Transferring Transferability: Towards a Theory for Size Generalization｡On Transferring Transferability: Towards a Theory for Size Generalization Eitan Levin⋄,,,\diamond Department of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, Caltech, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA. Yuxin Ma22footnotemark: 2⋄,,,\diamond Mateo Díaz Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics and the Mathematical Institute for Data Science, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD 21218, USA. Soledad Villar22footnotemark: 2 Abstract Many modern learning tasks require models that can take inputs of varying sizes. Consequently, dimension-independent architectures have been proposed for domains where the inputs are graphs, sets, and point clouds. Recent work on graph neural networks has explored whether a model trained on low-dimensional data can transfer its performance to higher-dimensional inputs. We extend this body of work by introducing a general framework for transferability across dimensions. We show that transferability corresponds precisely to continuity in a limit space formed by identifying small problem instances with equivalent large ones. This identification is driven by the data and the learning task. We instantiate our framework on existing architectures, and implement the necessary changes to ensure their transferability. Finally, we provide design principles for designing new transferable models. Numerical experiments support our findings. $\diamond$$\diamond$footnotetext: These authors contributed equally to this work Contents 1 Introduction 2 How to consistently grow: equivalence of differently sized objects 1. 2.1 How to define distances across dimensions 3 Transferability is just continuity 1. 4 Transferability implies size generalization 5 Transferable neural networks 5.1 Sets 5.2 Graphs 1. 5.3 Point clouds 6 Size generalization experiments Acknowledgments 1. B.3 Metrics on consistent sequences C Transferability: details and missing proofs from Section 3 C.1 Transferable maps C.2 Convergence, transferability and stability C.3 Convergence rates under sampling D Generalization bounds: details and missing proofs from Section 4 D.1 Transferable neural networks E Example 1 (sets): details and missing proofs from Section 5.1 E.1 Consistent sequences on sets E.2 Invariant networks on sets F Example 2 (graphs): details and missing proofs from Section 5.2 F.1 Duplication consistent sequence for graphs F.2 Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) F.3 Constructing new transferable GNNs: GGNN and continuous GGNN G Example 3 (point clouds): details and missing proofs from Section 5.3 G.1 Duplication consistent sequence for point clouds G.2 DeepSet for Conjugation Invariance (DS-CI) G.3 Constructing new transferable models: SVD-DS H Size generalization experiments: details from Section 6 H.1 Size generalization on sets H.2 Size generalization on graphs H.3 Size generalization on 3D point clouds H.4 Continuity of Gromov-Wasserstein distance and its third lower bound I Limitations of this work 1 Introduction Modern learning problems often involve inputs of arbitrary size: language has text sequences of arbitrary length, graphs encode networks with an arbitrary number of nodes, and particle systems might have an arbitrary number of points. Although traditional models are typically limited to the specific input dimensions they were trained on, dimension-independent architectures have been proposed for several domains. For instance, graph neural networks (GNN) for graphs [61], DeepSet for sets [82], and PointNet for point clouds [56]. These models have a desirable feature: they can be trained with low-dimensional samples and, then, deployed on higher-dimensional data. A key question in this context is whether the performance of a model trained with low-dimensional samples transfers across dimensions. This has been thoroughly studied in the context of GNNs [61, 50, 51], where the term transferability was first coined. In turn, the tools used to establish transferability of GNNs are, at first sight, problem-specific, including the concept of a graphon, and certain convergence of homomorphism densities. Thus, the analysis does not readily extend beyond GNNs, and so we ask What properties of the model, data, and learning task ensure that learning performance transfers well across dimensions? This question is relevant for the current pursuit of graph foundation models [46], GNN for combinatorial optimization [9], neural PDE solvers [57, 44], and so on, where pre-trained models aim to be adapted to a wide range of tasks involving different-sized objects.ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org2. Numerical experiments support our findings. ∗ Department of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, Caltech, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA. † Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics and the Mathematical Institute for Data Science, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD 21218, USA. ⋄ These authors contributed equally to this work 1 Contents 1 Introduction 3 2 How to consistently grow: equivalence of differently sized objects 5 2.1 How to define distances across dimensions 7 3 Transferability is just continuity 7 4 Transferability implies size generalization 8 5 Transferable neural networks 9 5.1 Sets 9 5.2 Graphs 10 5.3 Point clouds 11 6 Size generalization experiments 12 Acknowledgments 14 References 14 A Notation 19 B Consistent sequences and compatible, transferable maps: details and missing proofs from Section 2 20 C Transferability: details and missing proofs from Section 3 26 D Generalization bounds: details and missing proofs from Section 4 31 E Example 1 (sets): details and missing proofs from Section 5.1 35 F Example 2 (graphs): details and missing proofs from Section 5.2 44 G Example 3 (point clouds): details and missing proofs from Section 5.3 55 H Size generalization experiments: details from Section 6 62 I Limitations of this work 69 2 1 Introduction Modern learning problems often involve inputs of arbitrary size: language has text sequences of arbitrary length, graphs encode networks with an arbitrary number of nodes, and particle systems might have an arbitrary number of points. Although traditional models are typically limited to the specific input dimensions they were trained on, dimension-independent architectures have been proposed for several domains. For instance, graph neural networks (GNN) for graphs [61], DeepSet for sets [82], and PointNet for point clouds [56]. These models have a desirable feature: they can be trained with low-dimensional samples and, then, deployed on higher-dimensional data. A key question in this context is whether the performance of a model trained with low-dimensional samples transfers across dimensions. This has been thoroughly studied in the context of GNNs [61, 50, 51], where the term transferability was first coined. In turn, the tools used to establish transferability of GNNs are, at first sight, problem-specific, including the concept of a graphon, and certain convergence of homomorphism densities. Thus, the analysis does not readily extend beyond GNNs, and so we ask What properties of the model, data, and learning task ensure that learning performance transfers well across dimensions? This question is relevant for the current pursuit of graph foundation models [46], GNN for combinatorial optimization [9], neural PDE solvers [57, 44], and so on, where pre-trained models aim to be adapted to a wide range of tasks involving different-sized objects. In this paper, we answer this question by identifying assumptions on the learning problem that make a model generalize across dimensions, and give a theoretical framework to understand models with such properties. Our framework requires technical notions that we develop throughout the paper, so before diving into the details, we proceed to give the high-level intuition. Our framework considers a machine learning model parametrized by θ ∈ Rk, where the number of parameters k is fixed. For any fixed θ, the model can be evaluated on inputs of any size n. That is, the learned θ defines a sequence of functions, for example, (fn : Vn → R)n with increasingly larger input sizes.1 We think of Vn ⊆ V∞ as a subspace of an infinite-dimensional limit space.arxiv.org3. Any-dimensional equivariant neural networks — LacunaAny-dimensional equivariant neural networks — Lacuna｡Any-dimensional equivariant neural networks Eitan Levin, Mateo Díaz AISTATS 2024 · DBLP Standard neural networks are typically constrained to the input dimensions they were trained on. A model trained on 28×2828\times2828×28 images cannot natively process 50×5050\times5050×50 inputs without resizing or cropping. However, many fundamental problems—from physics to graph theory—are inherently dimension-agnostic. This paper introduces a framework for training "free" equivariant neural networks that generalize across dimensions by leveraging representation stability. The Challenge of Dimension-Agnostic Learning Many real-world mappings are naturally defined for any input size. For instance, the laws of physics apply regardless of the number of particles, and graph properties like "max-cut" are well-defined for any number of nodes. Most current architectures are "locked" into a specific dimension. This research addresses how to learn mappings that accept inputs of any dimension in a mathematically rigorous way, avoiding the "hacks" typically used to handle varying input sizes. Methodology: Equivariance and Stability The proposed framework combines two core concepts: Equivariance: Ensuring the model respects symmetries (e.g., if you permute particles, the output should permute or remain invariant). Representation Stability: A concept from algebraic topology suggesting that for certain group sequences (like permutations SnS_nSn), the structure of equivariant maps stabilizes as nnn grows. The "secret sauce" is a compatibility constraint (CompNNCompNNCompNN). The authors found that simply making a network extendable often leads to poor generalization. The compatibility condition ensures that applying the function in a low dimension is mathematically consistent with extending it to a high dimension and then applying it. The architecture of any-dimensional equivariant networks, showing how layers are lifted across dimensions while maintaining compatibility. Source, p. 3 The training process follows a four-stage "recipe": Identify Symmetry: Determine the relevant symmetry group (e.g., permutations for sets). Find Basis: Establish a basis for equivariant layers at a training dimension n0n_0n0. Train: Optimize the model on data of size n0n_0n0. Lift: To use the model on a new size nnn, solve a sparse linear system to "lift" the learned weights. Experimental Results The authors evaluated the approach on five synthetic tasks: Trace, Diagonal Extraction, Symmetric Projection, Top Singular Vector, and an Orthogonal Invariance task. Training was conducted at a small fixed dimension (e.g., d=4d=4d=4), and testing spanned a range of dimensions. Performance comparison across five tasks. The "Compatible" networks (blue) maintain low error across dimensions, while "Free" networks (orange) without the compatibility constraint fail significantly outside their training dimension (indicated by the vertical dashed line). Source, p. 8 The results demonstrate a stark contrast: Consistent Generalization: Compatible networks maintained low Mean Squared Error (MSE) (e.g., ∼10−8\sim 10^{-8}∼10−8 for Trace) across all tested dimensions. Failure of Naive Extension: Without the compatibility constraint, errors exploded by factors as high as 101010^{10}1010 when moving away from the training dimension. Stability Plateaus: The complexity of the mapping (e.g., the number of parameters) remains constant after a certain point, confirming that the "structure" of these problems stabilizes. Conclusion and Future Directions This framework provides a "black box" approach for any problem with known underlying symmetries. While powerful, it faces challenges in scaling to extremely high dimensions due to the need for solving large sparse linear systems. Future work aims to extend this to non-reductive groups (including translations) and to provide theoretical bounds on generalization error for any-dimensional problems.lacuna.tiptreesystems.com5. [Literature Review] Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization[Literature Review] Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization Moonlight｡[Literature Review] Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization TL;DR Solve length generalization issues with the new LDHD framework, enabling robust scaling from low-dimensional training to high-dimensional data. The paper "Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization and Its Implications for Length Generalization" by Yang Chen, Yitao Liang, and Zhouchen Lin explores a novel theoretical framework termed Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension (LDHD) generalization. This framework is positioned within the broader context of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization, highlighting the scaling challenges that arise when training models on low-dimensional data that must later generalize to high-dimensional spaces. Core Methodology The fundamental assumption guiding the approach is that instances of a problem can be represented as being generated from a latent variable. The dimensionality of this latent variable is suggested to correspond to the complexity or scale of a problem. The authors articulate a specific pathway by which challenges associated with length generalization—the ability to extend understanding from smaller, more manageable instances to larger, more complex ones—can be linked to this low-to-high dimensionality. In essence, the proposed LDHD generalization contextualizes the learning task as follows: Data Generation Process: The data generation for an instance of scale n n n takes place through: Sampling a latent variable h h h from a low-dimensional subspace Σn Σ^n Σn. Determining the output label y y y from this latent variable and an associated concept c c c, where y=c(h) y = c(h) y=c(h). Mapping h h h into a structured input sequence using a data format mapping ϕ ϕ ϕ. Generalizing from Low to High Dimensions: Training occurs with instances sampled from a lower-dimensional subspace, while testing is carried out in a larger, more complex high-dimensional superspace. This setup is characterized by an inherent mismatch, making it difficult for models to leverage learned experiences from training data when applied to testing scenarios. Theoretical Foundations The paper extends traditional definitions relevant to PAC learning theory to include this context of dimensional shifts. It derives a No-Free-Lunch Theorem specific to LDHD generalization, claiming that generalization across these dimensional domains cannot reliably be achieved without prior knowledge about the problem structure, which acts as an inductive bias effectively guiding learning. To substantiate this claim, the authors focus on the implications of different model architectures trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD), investigating their convergence properties and inductive biases. Notably, they explore how some architectures (like random feature models and their projections) capture concepts as min-degree interpolators—meaning they learn to represent functions with minimal polynomial degree necessary for accuracy. Empirical Studies and Model Architecture Central to their investigation is a detailed analysis of specific architectures under SGD such as: Random Feature Models with Projection: These models illustrate how transformations on input data can impact model convergence on certain functions—specifically showing that they converge on min-degree interpolators in relevant function classes. Position-Only Linear Attention with Advice (PLAA): An architecture that minimizes complexity by focusing purely on positional embeddings. The study shows that the reminiscences of understanding long-term dependencies of sequences diminish when using absolute position embeddings; this is remedied by implementing relative position embeddings, which have shown to foster generalization significantly. The outcomes from experiments compare models trained with varying position embedding strategies, notably distinguishing between standard relative position embeddings (RPE) and a novel adaptation termed RPE-Square. The latter is proposed to better handle the nuisances of data formats in the context of achieving length generalization—a key challenge elucidated through the theoretical insights of LDHD generalization. Summary of Contributions The paper presents several key contributions: It formalizes the LDHD generalization framework, tying it closely to length generalization challenges present in various reasoning tasks. Establishes the necessity of utilizing prior structure through appropriate inductive bias to achieve LDHD generalization. Delivers insights into how different model architectures interact with this generalization phenomenon, specifically under SGD optimizations. Proposes the RPE-Square, providing a specific solution targeting the nuances of data formats and general length reasoning. Ultimately, the authors contend that the LDHD framework not only helps clarify the intricacies associated with length generalization but also suggests actionable pathways for future model designs and embedding strategies directed at enhancing generalization capabilities across varied reasoning tasks. They outline implications for further research, particularly in refining inductive biases and developing robust models adaptable to complex generalization challenges.themoonlight.io6. Multilevel Diffusion: Infinite Dimensional Score-Based Diffusion Models for Image Generation — LacunaMultilevel Diffusion: Infinite Dimensional Score-Based Diffusion Models for Image Generation — Lacuna｡Multilevel Diffusion: Infinite Dimensional Score-Based Diffusion Models for Image Generation Paul Hagemann, Lars Ruthotto, Gabriele Steidl, Nicole Tianjiao Yang, Yang, Nicole Tianjiao arXiv 2023 · DOI · DBLP Abstract Traditional Score-Based Diffusion Models (SBDMs) are typically constrained to fixed-resolution image tensors, leading to theoretical inconsistencies and practical limitations when scaling to higher resolutions. This paper introduces a novel framework that formulates SBDMs in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. By utilizing trace-class covariance operators and resolution-independent Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs), the authors enable "multilevel training." This approach allows models to generalize across resolutions and provides a mathematically grounded method for warm-starting high-resolution training from low-resolution precursors. Introduction Most state-of-the-art generative models treat images as discrete, fixed-size grids (e.g., 32×3232 \times 3232×32 or 256×256256 \times 256256×256 pixels). While this approach has yielded impressive results, it tethers the model to a specific discretization. From a mathematical perspective, this formulation is ill-posed in the infinite-dimensional limit: as the number of pixels ddd approaches infinity, the energy of standard Gaussian noise (the trace of the identity matrix) also approaches infinity. Consequently, models trained at one resolution often fail to generalize to others without significant retraining or the use of heuristic upsamplers. To address this, the authors propose treating images as continuous functions residing in a separable Hilbert space. This shift from discrete tensors to continuous function spaces allows for a consistent mathematical framework that remains valid across any resolution. Theoretical Framework: Beyond the Identity Crisis The core innovation of this work lies in the definition of forward and reverse diffusion processes using Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) in infinite dimensions. The authors identify a primary culprit in the scaling failure of traditional models: the choice of identity covariance (Q=IdQ=IdQ=Id). In infinite dimensions, identity noise is not well-defined because it lacks a finite trace. To resolve this, the researchers replace the standard identity covariance with trace-class covariance operators. These operators, often based on the Laplacian or Bessel potentials, act as low-pass filters. They ensure that the latent noise distribution remains well-defined even as the resolution increases, effectively "taming" the noise energy in the infinite-dimensional limit. Resolution-Invariant Architectures Standard neural architectures like U-Nets are inherently sensitive to input resolution. To maintain the integrity of the infinite-dimensional formulation, the authors employ Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs). Unlike CNNs, FNOs learn mappings between function spaces by operating in the frequency domain. This allows the model to learn the underlying structure of the data (the "digit function") rather than just the pixel values. This architecture is naturally resolution-invariant, enabling the model to process inputs at any discretization level. Multilevel Training Strategy The authors introduce a multilevel training strategy to improve computational efficiency. The process involves: Training a model on coarse, low-resolution data. Using the weights of the low-resolution model as a "warm start" for training on finer, high-resolution data. This approach is theoretically supported by proofs showing that the discretized models converge to the true infinite-dimensional process. This ensures that the transition between resolutions is mathematically consistent rather than a mere empirical trick. Experimental Results The framework was evaluated across synthetic data, handwritten digits (MNIST), and complex physical simulations (2D Reaction-Diffusion equations). Zero-Shot Super-Resolution A significant finding was the model's capacity for zero-shot super-resolution. An FNO-based model trained exclusively on 32×3232 \times 3232×32 MNIST images successfully generated recognizable digits at 64×6464 \times 6464×64 and 128×128128 \times 128128×128 resolutions without any additional training. In contrast, standard U-Net architectures failed completely, producing only unstructured noise when tested at higher resolutions. Training Efficiency Multilevel training demonstrated clear practical benefits. In MNIST experiments, warm-starting a 64×6464 \times 6464×64 model with weights from a 32×3232 \times 3232×32 model reduced total training time by approximately 9% while maintaining or improving sample quality. This suggests a path toward more sustainable scaling of large generative models.lacuna.tiptreesystems.com7. Category Learning Stretches Neural Representations in Visual CortexCategory Learning Stretches Neural Representations in Visual Cortex｡Category Learning Stretches Neural Representations in Visual Cortex Abstract We review recent work that shows how learning to categorize objects changes how those objects are represented in the mind and the brain. After category learning, visual perception of objects is enhanced along perceptual dimensions that were relevant to the learned categories, an effect we call dimensional modulation (DM). DM stretches object representations along category-relevant dimensions and shrinks them along category-irrelevant dimensions. The perceptual advantage for category-relevant dimensions extends beyond categorization and can be observed during visual discrimination and other tasks that do not depend on the learned categories. fMRI shows that category learning causes ventral stream neural populations in visual cortex representing objects along a category-relevant dimension to become more distinct. These results are consistent with a view that specific aspects of cognitive tasks associated with objects can account for how our visual system responds to objects. Keywords: Categorization, Category Learning, Perceptual Learning, Face Recognition, fMRI Learning to group objects into categories is a basic biological function, letting us recognize visually different objects as the same kind. To categorize an object, the visual system must create a perceptual representation, that representation is then compared with learned category knowledge, and a categorization decision is made (e.g., see Richler & Palmeri, 2014). Cells in the ventral stream of the visual cortex are sensitive to both simple and complex visual features and dimensions (Ullman, Vidal-Naquet, & Sali, 2002). While evolutionary, genetic, and developmental mechanisms play key roles in shaping the properties of visual neurons, debate continues about the effect of experience on representations in the adult visual cortex. As predicted by some cognitive models, our recent work has shown how category learning optimizes neural representations in visual cortex to make discriminations useful for the cognitive tasks associated with learned objects. Category Learning Stretches Object Representations Many models of categorization assume that objects are represented along multiple psychological dimensions (Ashby, 1992; Richler & Palmeri, 2014). These dimensions can be psychophysically simple, like size or color (Goldstone, 1994), more complex but localized, like object parts (Nosofsky, 1986; Sigala & Logothetis, 2002), or global properties related to object shape (Folstein et al., 2012, 2013; Freedman et al., 2003; Goldstone & Steyvers, 2001; Gureckis & Goldstone 2008; Jiang et al. 2007). For object categories, certain dimensions may be more relevant than others. Imagine that members of one category have a particular shape and color while members of a different category have a different shape and color. In that case, shape and color would be relevant dimensions while other dimensions, like size and texture, would be irrelevant. A key assumption of many successful category-learning models (e.g., Kruschke, 1992; Nosofsky, 1984, 1986) is that relevant dimensions are more heavily weighted. This “stretches” psychological space along these dimensions, making objects that differ along them less similar to one another (Figures 1 and 2). We call the effect of this stretching dimensional modulation (DM) because object similarity is selectively modulated along category-relevant dimensions. Figure 1. While the flattened two-dimension representations are strikingly similar, the actual spaces of morphs and their relationships to the learned category boundaries are quite different, with consequences on observed behavior, as outlined in the text. Folstein, Department of Psychology, Florida State University, 1107 W. Van Gulick2 , and Isabel Gauthier2 1 Florida State University and 2 Vanderbilt University Abstract In this article, we review recent work that shows how learning to categorize objects changes how those objects are represented in the mind and the brain. After category learning, visual perception of objects is enhanced along perceptual dimensions that were relevant to the learned categories, an effect we call dimensional modulation. Dimensional modulation stretches object representations along category-relevant dimensions and shrinks them along category- irrelevant dimensions. The perceptual advantage for category-relevant dimensions extends beyond categorization and can be observed during visual discrimination and other tasks that do not depend on the learned categories. Evidence from fMRI studies shows that category learning causes ventral-stream neural populations in visual cortex representing objects along a category-relevant dimension to become more distinct. These results are consistent with a view that specific aspects of cognitive tasks associated with objects can account for how our visual system responds to objects. We can further contrast flexible and stable DM (Folstein, Gauthier, & Palmeri, 2012; Gauthier & Palmeri, 2002; Goldstone, 1998; Palmeri & Gauthier, 2004; Richler & Palmeri, 2014). DM can sometimes be viewed as the result of a flexible process, with dimension weights shift- ing in an optimal fashion depending on current task demands (Nosofsky, 1984, 1998). But DM can also be the result of a more stable, task-independent form of percep- tual learning in which diagnostic dimensions become perceptually more discriminable (e.g. Goldstone, 1994). The brain's ability to perceive space expands like the universeThe brain's ability to perceive space expands like the universe ScienceDaily｡Science News from research organizations Date: Source: Salk Institute Summary: Scientists have discovered that time spent exploring an environment causes neural representations to grow in surprising ways. This discovery provides valuable methods for analyzing data on neurocognitive disorders involving learning and memory, such as Alzheimer's disease. Share: FULL STORY Young children sometimes believe that the moon is following them, or that they can reach out and touch it. It appears to be much closer than is proportional to its true distance. As we move about our daily lives, we tend to think that we navigate space in a linear way. But Salk scientists have discovered that time spent exploring an environment causes neural representations to grow in surprising ways. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience on December 29, 2022, show that neurons in the hippocampus essential for spatial navigation, memory, and planning represent space in a manner that conforms to a nonlinear hyperbolic geometry -- a three-dimensional expanse that grows outward exponentially. (In other words, it's shaped like the interior of an expanding hourglass.) The researchers also found that the size of that space grows with time spent in a place. And the size is increasing in a logarithmic fashion that matches the maximal possible increase in information being processed by the brain. This discovery provides valuable methods for analyzing data on neurocognitive disorders involving learning and memory, such as Alzheimer's disease. "Our study demonstrates that the brain does not always act in a linear manner. Instead, neural networks function along an expanding curve, which can be analyzed and understood using hyperbolic geometry and information theory," says Salk Professor Tatyana Sharpee, holder of the Edwin K. Hunter Chair, who led the study. "It is exciting to see that neural responses in this area of the brain formed a map that expanded with experience based on the amount of time devoted in a given place. The effect even held for miniscule deviations in time when animal ran more slowly or faster through the environment." Sharpee's lab uses advanced computational approaches to better understand how the brain works. They recently pioneered the use of hyperbolic geometry to better understand biological signals like smell molecules, as well as the perception of smell. In the current study, the scientists found that hyperbolic geometry guides neural responses as well. Hyperbolic maps of sensory molecules and events are perceived with hyperbolic neural maps. The space representations dynamically expanded in correlation with the amount of time the rat spent exploring each environment. And, when a rat moved more slowly through an environment, it gained more information about the space, which caused the neural representations to grow even more. "The findings provide a novel perspective on how neural representations can be altered with experience," says Huanqiu Zhang, a graduate student in Sharpee's lab. "The geometric principles identified in our study can also guide future endeavors in understanding neural activity in various brain systems." "You would think that hyperbolic geometry only applies on a cosmic scale, but that is not true," says Sharpee. "Our brains work much slower than the speed of light, which could be a reason that hyperbolic effects are observed on graspable spaces instead of astronomical ones. Next, we would like to learn more about how these dynamic hyperbolic representations in the brain grow, interact, and communicate with one another." Other authors include P. Dylan Rich of Princeton University and Albert K. Lee of the Janelia Research Campus at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. The research was supported by an AHA-Allen Initiative in Brain Health and Cognitive Impairment award made jointly through the American Heart Association and the Paul G. Allen Frontiers Group (19PABH134610000), the Dorsett Brown Foundation, the Mary K. Chapman Foundation, an Aginsky Fellowship, the National Science Foundation (IIS-1724421), the National Science Foundation Next Generation Networks for Neuroscience Program (Award 2014217), the National Institutes of Health (U19NS112959 and P30AG068635), and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Journal Reference : Huanqiu Zhang, P. Dylan Rich, Albert K. Lee, Tatyana O. Sharpee. Hippocampal spatial representations exhibit a hyperbolic geometry that expands with experience . Effective learning is accompanied by high-dimensional and efficient representations of neural activity - Nature NeuroscienceEffective learning is accompanied by high-dimensional and efficient representations of neural activity - Nature Neuroscience｡Published: 20 May 2019 Effective learning is accompanied by high-dimensional and efficient representations of neural activity Evelyn Tang ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-8274-88501,2, Marcelo G. Mattar ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-3303-24903, Chad Giusti1,4, David M. Lydon-Staley1, Sharon L. Thompson-Schill3 & Danielle S. Bassett ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-6183-44931,5,6,7,8 Nature Neuroscience volume 22, pages 1000–1009 (2019)Cite this article Abstract A fundamental cognitive process is to map value and identity onto the objects we learn about. However, what space best embeds this mapping is not completely understood. Here we develop tools to quantify the space and organization of such a mapping in neural responses as reflected in functional MRI, to show that quick learners have a higher dimensional representation than slow learners, and hence more easily distinguishable whole-brain responses to objects of different value. Furthermore, we find that quick learners display more compact embedding of their neural responses, and hence have higher ratios of their stimuli dimension to their embedding dimension, which is consistent with greater efficiency of cognitive coding. Lastly, we investigate the neurophysiological drivers at smaller scales and study the complementary distinguishability of whole-brain responses. Our results demonstrate a spatial organization of neural responses characteristic of learning and offer geometric measures applicable to identifying efficient coding in higher-order cognitive processes.
